evidence_summary: The review identifies inertial measurement units and insole-based pressure systems as major wearable approaches used in fall-related research. These systems provide motion, gait, postural and plantar-pressure variables that can be analyzed for fall-risk assessment or fall detection, but the specific variables, sensor configurations and analysis methods differ across studies.

evidence_summary: The review identifies substantial variation in the parameters used for fall-risk assessment and in wearable sensor configurations. For insole systems, sensor size, number and placement also vary. The authors state that this lack of standardization can make comparison and clinically relevant interpretation difficult and recommend standardized protocols and consistent data management for fall-related studies.

results.reporting_notes: Table 1 reports descriptive output-rating outcomes. Q1 comparison reports a 40/50 win rate among nontied comparisons with 95% CI 67.0-88.8 and exploratory sign-test P<=.001; four ties were reported. These metrics must not be interpreted as sensitivity, specificity, AUC, or clinical fall-prediction accuracy.
results.result_summary: Enhanced system output was preferred in 40/54 ratings (74.1%). Enhanced-system unsafe/inappropriate recommendation rate was 0/54; visualization fidelity was 43/54 (79.6%); hazard-introducing or implausible edit rate was 6/54 (11.1%); actionability median was 5.0 on a 1-5 Likert scale. These are formative output-rating results, not fall-prediction performance.
